doc.title: Jim Cullum interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2007

title: Sweets Edison's Basie story and playing riffs without rehearsal
summary: Cullum tells Edison's story of finding a harmony note in Basie's band, and explains how his band finds riff notes by ear.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: Arrange it a little more. And sometimes they didn’t have any music, you just go with what you can sort of listen for another harmony note. We had Sweets Edison on the show one time and he told a story about playing with Basie and he says he went into Basie and he says, “I’m frustrated” he says, “I’m going to have to give my notice.” And so Basie says, “Why, you sound real good,” he says, “what’s the problem?” He says, “I can’t find a note, I can’t find a note.” There was all the other guys that had all the notes from the rhythm, and he can’t find a harmony note to harmonize a note to the riff.

You’ve got this big band going on there. And he says so Basie says, “Well you sound real good, I love the way you play,” he says, “let me just say if you find a note tonight play the same damn note every night.”
He’s trying to find a note. You find that note keep playing it. Well anyway — © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -3-
But the guys next to him wouldn’t want, they don’t want him to have their note.
No. Get off my note. Get off my note.
There’s only so many notes. Try the second alto player’s note.

That’s right. So anyway, the life of the riff things. So sometimes you’re playing riffs in harmony like that. With three horns it’s pretty easy to riff and find a note. It’s easy. It’s pretty easy to get a note.
Do you guys rehearse that kind of thing?

Usually we don’t. Sometimes we’re standing up there playing and I’ll say to the clarinet player I’m going to play this pattern [scats] and I’ll say I’ll start on the G or whatever it is, so then he’ll know. And then maybe he says to the trombone player, “Start on the B flat” or something. So everybody just listens and then fall — you’d be amazed at how fast they fall into it. And of course we do it all the time. And it’s what makes the music fun and fresh and spontaneous and full of life, and all of that stuff.
